title: One king, appointed by God and not by the son of Cronus
source_text: Εἶθ᾿ ἑξῆς φησιν ὁ Κέλσος ὅτι οὐ χρὴ ἀπιστεῖν ἀνδρὶ ἀρχαίῳ, πάλαι προειπόντι τό· εἷς βασιλεὺς, ᾧ ἔδωκε Κρόνου παῖς ἀγκυλομήτεω. καὶ ἐπιφέρει· ὡς, ἂν τοῦτο λύσῃς τὸ δόγμα, εἰκότως ἀμυνεῖταί σε ὁ βασιλεύς. εἰ γὰρ τὸ αὐτό σοι ποιήσειαν ἅπαντες, οὐδὲν κωλύσει τὸν μὲν καταλειφθῆναι μόνον καὶ ἔρημον, τὰ δ᾿ ἐπὶ γῆς ἐπὶ τοῖς ἀνομωτάτοις τε καὶ ἀγριωτάτοις βαρβάροις γενέσθαι, καὶ μήτε τῆς σῆς θρησκείας μήτε τῆς ἀληθινῆς σοφίας ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἔτι καταλείπεσθαι κλέος. εἷς μὲν οὖν κοίρανος ἔστω, εἷς βασιλεὺς, οὐχ ᾧ ἔδωκε Κρόνου παῖς ἀγκυλομήτεω, ἀλλ᾿ ᾧ ἔδωκεν ὁ καθιστῶν „βασιλεῖς καὶ“ μεθιστῶν „καὶ τὸν χρήσιμον“ κατὰ καιρὸν ἐγείρων ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς· καὶ οὐχ ὁ τοῦ καταταρταρωθέντος, ὡς οἱ μῦθοι Ἑλλήνων λέγρυσι, Κρόνου υἱὸς ἀπελάσας τοῦτον τῆς ἀρχῆς καθίστησι βασιλεῖς, οὐδ᾿ ἂν ἀλληγορῇ τις τὰ κατὰ τοὺς τόπους, ἀλλ᾿ ὁ διοικῶν τὰ σύμπαντα θεὸς οἶδεν ὅ τι ποτὲ ποιεῖ κατὰ τὸν τόπον τῆς τῶν βασιλέων καταστάσεως. λύομεν οὖν τὸ δόγμα· ᾧ ἔδωκε Κρόνου παῖς ἀγκυλομήτεω, οὐδὲν ἀγκύλον καὶ σκολιὸν βούλεσθαι πειθόμενοι θεὸν ἢ πατέρα θεοῦ. οὐ λύομεν δὲ τὸ δόγμα τὸ περὶ προνοίας καὶ τῶν εἴτε προηγουμένως ὑπ᾿ αὐτῆς γινομένων εἴτε καὶ ἔκ τινων ἐπακολουθούντων. ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿ εἰκότως ἡμᾶς ἀμύνεται βασιλεὺς, φάσκοντας μὲν ὅτι οὐ Κρόνου παῖς ἀγκυλομήτεω ἔδωκεν αὐτῷ τὸ βασιλεύειν, ὁ δὲ μεθιστῶν „βασιλεῖς καὶ“ καθιστῶν. καὶ τὸ αὐτό γε ποιείτωσάν μοι ἅπαντες, τὸ μὲν Ὁμηρικὸν καταλύοντες δόγμα τὸ δὲ θεῖον περὶ βασιλέως τηροῦντες καὶ τὸ „τὸν βασιλέα τιμᾶτε“ φυλάττοντες· καὶ τὸ ὡς ἐν ὑποθέσει γε τοιαύτῃ οὔτε μόνος ὁ βασιλεὺς καταλειφθήσεται οὔτ᾿ ἔρημος ἔσται οὔτε τὰ ἐπὶ γῆς ἐπὶ τοῖς ἀνομωτάτοις καὶ ἀγριωτάτοις βαρβάροις ἔσται. εἰ γὰρ, ὡς λέγει Κέλσος, τὸ αὐτό μοι ποιήσειαν ἅπαντες, δηλονότι καὶ οἱ βάρβαροι τῷ λόγῳ τοῦ θεοῦ προσελθόντες νομιμώτατοι ἔσονται καὶ ἡμερώτατοι· καὶ πᾶσα μὲν θρησκεία καταλυθήσεται μόνη δὲ ἡ Χριστιανῶν κρατήσει, ἥτις καὶ μόνη ποτὲ κρατήσει, τοῦ λόγου ἀεὶ πλείονας νεμομένου ψυχάς.
pass_a_gloss: Then next Celsus says that one must not disbelieve (ἀπιστέω) an ancient man who long ago foretold/declared (προλέγω) this: 'One king, to whom the son of crooked-counselling (ἀγκυλομήτης) Cronus gave (it).' And he adds: 'Since, if you undo (λύω) this doctrine (δόγμα), the king will reasonably/rightly (εἰκότως) punish (ἀμύνομαι) you. For if all were to do the same as you, nothing will prevent him from being left (καταλείπω) alone and deserted (ἔρημος), and the things on earth from coming to (ἐπί + dat.) the most lawless (ἀνομώτατος) and most savage (ἀγριώτατος) barbarians, and neither of your worship (θρησκεία) nor of the true wisdom (σοφία) any glory (κλέος) still to be left among men.' Let there be then one lord (κοίρανος), one king, not to whom the son of crooked-counselling Cronus gave, but to whom gave the one who sets up (καθίστημι) 'kings and' removes (μεθίστημι), 'and the useful one (χρήσιμος)' at the right time (κατὰ καιρόν) raising up (ἐγείρω) 'over the earth'; and not the son of Cronus who was cast into Tartarus (καταταρταρόω), as the myths of the Greeks say, having driven him from rule (ἀρχή), appoints kings, not even if someone allegorises (ἀλληγορέω) the things in the passages; but God governing (διοικέω) all things knows what he does in the matter of the appointment (κατάστασις) of kings. We undo then the doctrine 'to whom the son of crooked-counselling Cronus gave', persuaded (πείθομαι) that God or a father of God wills (βούλομαι) nothing crooked (ἀγκύλος) and twisted (σκολιός). But we do not undo the doctrine about providence and about the things coming about by it either primarily/antecedently (προηγουμένως) or from certain consequent things (ἐπακολουθέω). But neither does a king reasonably punish us, saying that not the son of crooked-counselling Cronus gave him kingship, but the one removing 'kings and' setting up. And let all do the same (as) me (μοι), undoing the Homeric doctrine but keeping (τηρέω) the divine (doctrine) about the king and guarding (φυλάττω) the 'Honour (τιμάω) the king'; and in such a hypothesis (ὑπόθεσις) neither will the king be left alone nor be deserted, nor will the things on earth be to the most lawless and most savage barbarians. For if, as Celsus says, all were to do the same as I, clearly the barbarians too, having come to the word/Word (λόγος) of God, will be most law-abiding (νομιμώτατος) and most gentle (ἡμερώτατος); and all worship (θρησκεία) will be undone (καταλύω) and only that of the Christians will prevail (κρατέω), which also alone will at some time prevail, the Word always possessing/spreading over (νέμομαι) more souls.
pass_b_english: Next Celsus says that one must not disbelieve an ancient man who long ago declared: “One king, to whom the son of crooked-counselling Cronus gave it” (Homer, Iliad 2.205). And he adds: “For if you overthrow this teaching, the king will rightly punish you. For if all were to do the same as you, nothing would prevent him from being left alone and deserted, and the affairs of the earth from falling into the hands of the most lawless and savage barbarians, and nothing would keep the fame of your religion, or of the true wisdom, from vanishing from among men.”

Let there be, then, “one lord, one king” (Homer, Iliad 2.204–205); not one “to whom the son of crooked-counselling Cronus gave it,” but one to whom He gave it who “sets up kings and removes them” (Daniel 2:21) and at the right time raises up “the man who is useful” over the earth (Sirach 10:4). And it is not the son of Cronus who appoints kings, the son who drove from his rule the father who, as the myths of the Greeks say, was cast down into Tartarus; nor is it so even if someone allegorises what is said in those passages. Rather, God who governs all things knows what He is doing in the matter of the appointment of kings.

We do overthrow, then, the teaching “to whom the son of crooked-counselling Cronus gave it,” since we are persuaded that neither a god nor a father of a god wills anything crooked or twisted. But we do not overthrow the teaching about providence, and about the things that come about by it either as its primary purpose or as consequences that follow from certain other things. Nor would a king rightly punish us for saying that it was not the son of crooked-counselling Cronus who gave him his kingship, but He who “removes kings and sets them up” (Daniel 2:21).

Yes, let all do the same as I do, overthrowing the Homeric teaching while keeping the divine teaching about the king and observing the words, “Honour the king” (1 Peter 2:17). On such a supposition the king will not be left alone, nor will he be deserted, nor will the affairs of the earth fall to the most lawless and savage barbarians. For if, as Celsus says, all were to do the same as I do, clearly the barbarians too, when they come to the Word of God, will be most law-abiding and most gentle; and every religion will be abolished, and that of the Christians alone will prevail. And indeed it alone will one day prevail, since the Word is always winning more and more souls.

choices.choice: The Homeric line is Iliad 2.205 (context 2.204-205: ‘Rule of many is not good; let there be one lord, one king, to whom the son of crooked-counselling Cronus gave...’); Origen’s ‘one lord, one king’ takes up 2.204-205 and is cited inline there. Daniel 2:21 follows the Theodotion text (μεθιστᾷ βασιλεῖς καὶ καθιστᾷ); Origen quotes it in two word orders, first ‘sets up kings and removes’ (ὁ καθιστῶν βασιλεῖς καὶ μεθιστῶν), then the biblical order ‘removes kings and sets up’ (ὁ μεθιστῶν βασιλεῖς καὶ καθιστῶν); the English follows Origen’s order each time. Sirach 10:4 (‘he will raise up the useful man in due season over it’, i.e. the earth). ‘neither a god nor a father of a god’ renders θεὸν ἢ πατέρα θεοῦ: Origen answers the epithet given to Cronus, father of Zeus; the phrase could also be read ‘God or the Father of God’ in a Christian sense; the more neutral pagan-facing reading is chosen and kept lowercase; doubtful. ‘λύω τὸ δόγμα’ rendered ‘overthrow the teaching’ throughout to keep Celsus’s verb and Origen’s reply aligned. προηγουμένως / ἐπακολουθούντων: the philosophical distinction between what providence intends primarily and what follows as a by-product. In ‘τὸ αὐτό γε ποιείτωσάν μοι ἅπαντες’ and ‘τὸ αὐτό μοι ποιήσειαν’ the dative goes with τὸ αὐτό (‘the same as I’): Origen turns Celsus’s ‘the same as you’ (τὸ αὐτό σοι) to himself. The text at ‘καὶ τὸ ὡς ἐν ὑποθέσει γε τοιαύτῃ’ is awkward; rendered by sense. The misprint λέγρυσι in the staged text is read as λέγουσι. ‘nothing would keep the fame ... from vanishing’ renders the last infinitive clause under οὐδὲν κωλύσει (μήτε ... μήτε ... ἔτι καταλείπεσθαι κλέος).
Celsus's last clause tied back to 'nothing would prevent' (μήτε ... καταλείπεσθαι κλέος depends on οὐδὲν κωλύσει); 'glory' -> 'fame' (κλέος)
'one lord, one king' put in quotation marks with (Homer, Iliad 2.204–205)
first Daniel 2:21 quotation now follows Origen's own order 'sets up kings and removes them' (was silently swapped to the biblical order)
Sirach 10:4 quotation marks narrowed to the words Origen quotes ('the man who is useful')
Tartarus sentence untangled: 'it is not the son of Cronus who appoints kings, the son who drove from his rule the father who ... was cast down into Tartarus'
'let all, I say, do the same as I do' -> 'Yes, let all do the same as I do' (μοι goes with τὸ αὐτό; 'I say' was a double rendering); note corrected
Iliad 2.205, Daniel 2:21 (Theodotion), Sirach 10:4, 1 Peter 2:17 checked: correct

choices.issue: open doubt for the owner (not a blocker)
choices.choice: 8.68: θεὸν ἢ πατέρα θεοῦ is kept as lowercase 'neither a god nor a father of a god', the pagan-facing reading. A Christian reading, 'God or the Father of God', is possible and is flagged as doubtful in the notes. Passed.
